Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 6–8:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their footsteps﴾, has two interpretations. The first: "killing yourself" (qatil nafsaka). From this is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

Ah, you who destroy yourself with grief for a thing the decrees have carved out of your hands.

The second: al-bakhi' (the one who destroys himself) is the one who is consumed with regret and sorrow. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿Over their footsteps﴾ has two interpretations. The first: over the traces of their disbelief.

The second: after their death.

﴿If they do not believe in this discourse, out of sorrow﴾ means: if the disbelievers of Quraysh do not believe in this discourse, meaning the Qur'an.

﴿Asaf (sorrow)﴾ has four interpretations. The first: meaning anger, said by Qatadah.

The second: distress, said by Mujahid.

The third: grief, said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: sadness, said by al-Hasan. And the poet has said:

I see a man among them, grieved, as if he were clasping to his sides a dyed hand.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it﴾ has five interpretations. The first: that it refers to the trees and rivers with which God adorned the earth, said by Muqatil.

The second: that it refers to men, because they are the adornment of the earth, said by al-Kalbi.

The third: that it refers to the prophets and scholars, said by al-Qasim.

The fourth: that everything on the earth is an adornment for it, said by Mujahid.

The fifth: that the meaning of ﴿an adornment for it﴾ is desires for its people, which are made attractive in their eyes and souls.

﴿That We may test them: which of them is best in deed﴾ has three interpretations. The first: which of them is best in turning away from it and abandoning it, said by Ibn 'Ata'.

The second: which of them is best in relying on Us regarding it, said by Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah.

The third: which of them is purest of heart and best in conduct.

It may also bear a fourth meaning: that We test them as to which of them is most inclined to take lessons from it.

And it may bear a fifth meaning: that We test them as to their avoidance of the forbidden within it.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And indeed, We will make what is on it a bare, barren wasteland﴾. Regarding al-sa'id (the surface of the earth) there are three sayings. The first: the level earth, said by al-Akhfash and Muqatil.

The second: it is the surface of the earth because of its rising (sa'ud), said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The third: that it is dust, said by Aban ibn Taghlib.

And regarding al-juruz (barren) there are four interpretations. The first: barren (balqa'), said by Mujahid.

The second: smooth (mal'a'), which is the saying of Muqatil.

The third: enclosed (mahsurah), which is the saying of Ibn Bahr.

The fourth: that it is dry land in which there is neither plant nor crop. The reciter said:

The lean years have swept them away.

[p. 287] The words of the Most High: ﴿Or do you think that the Companions of the Cave and the Inscription were among Our signs a wonder?﴾ As for the Cave (al-Kahf), it is a cave in the mountain to which the group retreated.

As for the Inscription (al-Raqim), there are seven opinions about it. The first: it is the name of the town they came from. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it is the name of the mountain. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The third: it is the name of the valley. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

'Ata' al-'Awfi said: it is a valley in Syria near Ayla. It has also been narrated that the name of the mountain of the Cave was Banajlus, the name of the Cave was Mirim, the name of the city was Afsus, and the name of the king was Wufyanus.

The fourth: it is the name of their dog. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. It has also been said that it is a name for every cave.

The fifth: the Inscription is the book in which their affair was written. This is the view of Mujahid, and it is derived from *al-raqm* (embroidery or marking) on cloth. It has also been said that the book was a lead tablet at the entrance of the Cave, and it has been said that it was kept in the treasuries of kings because of the wondrousness of their story.

The sixth: al-Raqim is the inkwell in Greek (*al-Rumiyya*). This is the view of Abu Salih.

The seventh: the Inscription is a people from among the Shurat (a group of people) whose condition was like the condition of the Companions of the Cave. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

﴿They were among Our signs a wonder﴾: there are two interpretations of this. The first: its meaning is, "Did you not suppose that they were a wonder among Our signs, were it not that We informed you and revealed it to you?" The second: its meaning is, "Did you suppose that they were the most wondrous of Our signs, when they are not the most wondrous of Our creation?" This is the view of Mujahid.

The words of the Most High: ﴿When the young men retreated to the cave﴾. There is a difference of opinion about the cause of their retreat to it, on two views. The first: they were people who fled with their religion to the cave. This is the view of al-Hasan.

﴿Then they said: Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself and prepare for us right guidance in our affair.﴾ The second: they were the sons of nobles and notables who went out and gathered behind the city without any prior arrangement. Then the eldest of them said, "I find in myself something that I do not think anyone else finds: indeed my Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth." So they all said, ﴿Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth; we will never call upon any god besides Him; we would then have uttered an excessive transgression.﴾ Then they entered the cave, where they remained three hundred years and nine more. This is the view of Mujahid.

Ibn Qutaybah said: they were sons of the Romans who entered the cave before 'Isa (Jesus). Allah placed a seal over their ears within it. When Allah sent 'Isa, He informed him of their story. Then Allah raised them up after 'Isa, in the interval between him and the Prophet (ﷺ).

Regarding ﴿shatatan﴾ there are three interpretations: the first: falsehood. This is the view of Qatadah. The second: exaggeration. This is the view of al-Akhfash. The third: injustice. This is the view of al-Dahhak.

The words of the Most High: ﴿So We struck over their ears in the cave for a number of years.﴾ Striking over the ears means preventing hearing, which indicates that they did not die but were asleep. Regarding ﴿years, a number﴾ there are two interpretations: the first: counted. The second: full years, with no months or days in them.

Allah struck over their ears, even though this is not among the causes of sleep, so that they would not hear what might wake them from their sleep.

The words of the Most High: ﴿Then We woke them up﴾, the verse.

By "resurrection" (*al-ba'th*) is meant waking them from their sleep.

﴿That We might know﴾, that is, that We might observe, ﴿which of the two parties was most precise in computing the time they had remained﴾. There are three interpretations: the first: in number. This is the view of Mujahid. The second: in term. This is the view of Muqatil. The third: in limit. This is the view of Qutrub.

Regarding "the two parties" there are four opinions:

The first: the two parties are those who differed about their affair from among the people of the young men. This is the view of Mujahid.

The second: one of the two parties is the young men, and the second is those who were present with them from the people of that time.

The third: one of the two parties is believers and the other is disbelievers.

The fourth: one of the two parties is Allah the Most High and the other is the creation, and the implied meaning is: "Are you more knowledgeable, or is Allah?"

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 13–16:

His saying, may He be glorified and exalted: ﴿And We strengthened their hearts﴾, has two interpretations. The first: We made them firm (thabbatnaha).

The second: We inspired them with patience (alhamnaha sabran), as related by al-Yazidi.

﴿Indeed, we would have spoken an enormity (shatatan)﴾ has two interpretations. The first: excess (ghuluwwan).

The second: remoteness (tabaduan).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Why do they not bring for them a clear authority?﴾ has three interpretations. The first: with a clear proof, as related by Muqatil.

The second: with a clear excuse, as related by Qatadah.

The third: with a clear book, as related by al-Kalbi.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He will facilitate for you from your affair a means of ease (mirfaqan)﴾ has two interpretations. The first: spaciousness.

The second: livelihood.

It may also bear a third meaning: namely, deliverance (khalasan). It is read as mirfaqan with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa, and as mirfaqan with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the fa. The difference between them is that with a kasra on the mim and a fatha on the fa, it refers to what reaches you from others, and with a fatha on the mim and a kasra on the fa, it refers to what reaches others from you.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And you would see the sun, when it rose, inclining away from their cave to the right, and when it set, passing them on the left﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it turns away from them, so that it does not strike them.

The second: it veers away from their cave to the right.

﴿And when it set, passing them on the left﴾. Regarding this there are three sayings. The first: the meaning of taqriduhum (passing them) is tuhadhihim (running alongside them), and al-qard (qard) is al-muhadhah (being parallel to), as said by al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'.

The second: its meaning is tuqatti'uhum dhat al-shimal, i.e., it passes them while deviating from them, from your saying qaradtuhu bil-miqradh, meaning I cut it (with the scissors).

The third: its meaning is that it gives them a small portion of its rays and then takes it back as it departs, derived from the clipping of dirhams that are returned, because they were in a desolate place. It was also said that this is because there was no roof over them to shade them; had the sun risen directly upon them, it would have burned them.

Regarding its deviation from them at rising and setting there are two opinions. The first: because their cave faced the Banat Na'sh (the stars of the Great Bear), so the sun did not strike it at sunrise or at sunset, as said by Muqatil.

The second: that God, exalted is He, turned the sun away from them so that their bodies would remain intact and be a lesson for whoever sees them or whose report reaches them.

(p-291) ﴿And they were in a spacious place (fajwah) from it﴾. Regarding this there are four sayings. The first: it means in an open space from it, as said by Qatadah.

The second: inside it, as said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: that it is the desolate place.

The fourth: that it is a wide area, as said by al-Akhfash, and from it is the saying of the poet:

"We filled every valley and fajwah
with men and horses, neither reluctant nor forsaking."

God Most High says: ﴿And you would think them awake, while they are asleep.﴾ *Al-Ayqaz* means those who are awake.

The *rajiz* (a poet composing in the *rajaz* meter) said:

*They found their brothers awake, and the sword was furious with them, furiously so.*

*Al-Ruqud* means those who are asleep.

It is said that their eyes were open, that they breathed, and that they did not speak.

﴿And We turn them to the right and to the left.﴾ This means the turning of sleepers, for if they were not turned, the earth would consume them because of their long stay.

It is also said that they were turned twice a year, six months on one side and six months on the other side. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him).

Mujahid said: They were turned only nine years after three hundred years, during which they were not turned.

Regarding the reason for which you think them awake while they are asleep, there are two views. The first: because their eyes are open. The second: because of their being turned to the right and to the left.

﴿And their dog stretched out its two forelegs at the threshold.﴾ Regarding ﴿their dog﴾ there are two views. The first: that it was a dog among the dogs that was with them, and this is the view of the majority. It is said that its name was Humran.

The second: that it was a human being among the people who was their cook and followed them. It was said, rather, that he was a shepherd.

Regarding ﴿at the threshold (al-wasid)﴾ there are five interpretations. The first: that it is the doorstep. The second: that it is the courtyard, as said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The third: that it is the enclosure, related by al-Yazidi. The fourth: that *al-wasid* and *al-saʿid* both mean dust, as said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr. The fifth: that it is the door, as said by ʿAtiyya. The poet said:

*In a wide land whose gate is not shut, and whose entrance I know well, and my being known there is not disowned.*

Jarir ibn ʿUbayd related that it was a small, young dog. Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: It was yellowish in color.

﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight, and you would have been filled with dread of them.﴾ Regarding this there are two aspects. The first: because of the length of their nails and hair, dread of them seizes the one who sees them, out of fear. The second: because of the awe that Allah Most High put upon them, which turns eyes away from them, so that no one would reach them until the Decree reaches its appointed term concerning them.

Saʿid ibn Jubayr related from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: I went on a campaign with Muʿawiya (may Allah be pleased with him) in the Sea of the Romans. We reached the cave in which the Companions of the Cave were. Muʿawiya said: I want to enter upon them and look at them. I said: This is not for you, for Allah has prevented one better than you from doing so. He, Exalted, says: ﴿If you had looked upon them, you would have turned away from them in flight﴾, and so on, the verse.

He sent a group of men to them, and when they entered the cave, Allah sent upon them a wind that expelled them.

It is also said that this miracle from their people was for a prophet, who is said to have been one of them, and he was the leader whom they followed and believed in.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 19–20:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And thus We raised them﴾ meaning: their being roused from their sleep.

Muqatil said: God also made their dog sleep along with them.

﴿So that they might question one another. A speaker among them said, "How long have you remained?"﴾ so that they might know the extent of their sleep.

﴿They said, "We have remained a day or part of a day."﴾ The one who asked was one of them, and the one who answered was another. He said "a day" because it is the longest usual duration of sleep. Then, when he saw that the sun had not set, he said ﴿or part of a day﴾, because they had been put to sleep at the beginning of the day and roused at its end.

﴿They said, "Your Lord knows best how long you have remained."﴾ There are two views regarding the speaker:

(p-294) One: it is a report from God, Exalted, that He knows best the length of their stay.

The second: it is the saying of their eldest, Maksilmina, when he saw the young men disagreeing about it, so he said, ﴿Your Lord knows best how long you have remained,﴾ thus speaking the truth and referring the matter to God, the All-Knowing. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas.

﴿So send one of you with this silver coin of yours to the city﴾ It is recited with a kasra and with a sukun on the rā' (wariqikum / warqikum); in both recitations it means dirhams (silver coins). As for al-warq with a fatha on the rā', it means camels and sheep. The poet said:

؎ It is You I call upon, so accept my supplication; expiate my sins and multiply my warq (wealth).

He means his camels and sheep.

﴿Let him look to see which is the purest food﴾ There are four interpretations of this: One: which of them has more food; this is the view of Ikrimah.

The second: which of them is more lawful as food; this is the view of Qatadah.

The third: which is better food; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The fourth: which is cheaper food.

﴿and let him bring you provision from it﴾ There are two possibilities: One: with what you are provided to eat.

The second: with what is lawful for you to eat.

﴿and let him be discreet﴾ This may carry two meanings: One: and let him seek the cheapest price.

The second: and let him be discreet in concealing your affair.

This indicates the permissibility of a group sharing their food even if some of them eat more, which is called al-munahadah, and which was considered disgraceful in the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period), so the Shari'ah came with its permission.

(p-295) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿For if they gain the upper hand over you, they will stone you﴾ There are three interpretations of this: One: they will stone you with their hands, in denunciation of you; this was said by al-Hasan.

The second: with their tongues, in backbiting and reviling you; this was said by Ibn Juraij.

The third: they will kill you.

Rajm (stoning) means killing, because it is one of its causes.

﴿or return you to their religion﴾ meaning, to their disbelief.

﴿and in that case you will never succeed, ever﴾ if they return you to their religion.

The third: which is better food; this was said by al-Kalbi.

The fourth: which is cheaper food.

﴿and let him bring you provision from it﴾ There are two possibilities: One: with what you are provided to eat.

The second: with what is lawful for you to eat.

﴿and let him be discreet﴾ This may carry two meanings: One: and let him seek the cheapest price.

The second: and let him be discreet in concealing your affair.

This indicates the permissibility of a group sharing their food even if some of them eat more, which is called al-munahadah, and which was considered disgraceful in the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic period), so the Shari'ah came with its permission.

(p-295) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿For if they gain the upper hand over you, they will stone you﴾ There are three interpretations of this: One: they will stone you with their hands, in denunciation of you; this was said by al-Hasan.

The second: with their tongues, in backbiting and reviling you; this was said by Ibn Juraij.

The third: they will kill you.

Rajm (stoning) means killing, because it is one of its causes.

﴿or return you to their religion﴾ meaning, to their disbelief.

﴿and in that case you will never succeed, ever﴾ if they return you to their religion.

The Qur'anic phrase (ﷺ) is not used here; the passage reads as follows.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And thus We caused them to be discovered﴾. There are two interpretations of this. The first: We made the people of their city aware of them (lit. We made the people of their city prevail over them). The second: We informed them of Our mercy.

And ﴿that they might know that the promise of Allah is true﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: that the people of their city might know that Allah's promise is true concerning the Hour and the return of creation to life, because He who put them to sleep like the dead for this extraordinary period, then woke them alive, is able to revive whom He caused to die and placed in the grave. The second: its meaning is that the People of the Cave, after their knowledge, might see that Allah's promise of their resurrection is true.

﴿When they disputed among themselves about their affair﴾. The explanation is that when they sent one of them with their silver coins to the city to bring them food and provisions, the people were astonished at his appearance and his coins were regarded as strange, due to the long passage of time. He was brought before the king, who was righteous and had believed, along with those who were with him. When he looked at him, he said: "Perhaps this is one of the youths who went out in the time of the king Decianus (Diqyanus). I have been asking Allah to show them to us." He asked the youth, who informed him, and so he set off with the people accompanying him to them. When they drew near the People of the Cave and the youths heard their speech, they feared them, and they urged one another to keep to their religion. When they entered upon them, Allah caused them to die the death of truth. Then the dispute which Allah, Exalted is He, mentioned concerning them occurred.

(p-296) Regarding their dispute there are two views. The first: they disputed whether they were alive or dead. The second: after knowing of their death, they disputed whether to build a structure over them by which they would be known, or to take a place of worship (masjid) over them.

It was also said: the king intended to bury them in a chest of gold. Then one of them came to him in a dream and said: "You intended to place us in a chest of gold, so do not do that, for we were created from dust and to it we shall return, so leave us alone."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verse 22:

(p-297) His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿They will say, "They were three, the fourth of them being their dog." And they will say, "They were five, the sixth of them being their dog," guessing at the unseen. And they will say, "They were seven, and the eighth of them was their dog."﴾ Here He placed the conjunction waw (and) to mark the break in the narrative, because the report had already been completed.

﴿Say, "My Lord knows best their number; none knows them except a few."﴾ Regarding those who differed about their number, there are two opinions. The first: they were the people of the city before it became known about them. The second: they were the People of the Book after a long time had passed since them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿guessing at the unseen﴾. Qatadah said: "Casting by way of conjecture." Zuhayr said:

Verse: "War is only what you know and have tasted, and it is not, concerning it, a report that is conjectured (rujjim)."

Ibn Abbas said: "I am among the few whom God Exalted excepted: they were seven, and the eighth of them was their dog."

Ibn Juraij and Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "They were eight," and they took His saying Exalted is He, ﴿and the eighth of them was their dog﴾, to mean: the owner of their dog.

Their people wrote down their names when they disappeared, and when their matter became clear, their names were inscribed over the entrance of the cave.

Ibn Juraij said: Their names were Maksilmina, Yimlikha, who was the one who went with the silver to buy food; Matrunas, Mahsaymilnina, Kashutush, Batlanus, Yutunas, and Bayrunas.

(p-298) Muqatil said: The dog belonged to Maksilmina, who was the eldest of them and was a owner of sheep.

﴿So do not argue concerning them except with an outward argument﴾. In this there are five aspects. The first: except what We have made clear to you of their matter; this was said by Mujahid. The second: what We have related to you of their affair is sufficient for you, so do not ask Me about the disclosure of anything other than it; this was said by Qatadah. The third: "except with an outward argument" means with a clear proof and a truthful report; this was said by Ali ibn Isa. The fourth: do not dispute concerning them with anyone, except that you relate to them a narration; this was said by Ibn Abbas. The fifth: it means that you call the people to witness against them.

﴿And do not seek a ruling concerning them from any of them﴾. In this there are two aspects. The first: do not seek a ruling, O Muhammad, concerning them from anyone of the People of the Book; this was said by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah. The second: it is an address to the Prophet ﷺ and a prohibition for his community.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 23–24:**

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And never say of anything, "Indeed, I will do that tomorrow,"﴾ ﴿unless [you add], "If Allah wills."﴾ Al-Akhfash (the grammarian) said: There is an ellipsis in it, and its estimated form is: "Unless you say, 'If Allah wills.'" Although this is phrased as a command, it is meant as instruction and guidance: that you should not resolve upon a matter unless you attach to it the will of Allah, the Exalted, for two reasons.

The first: resolve may be turned away by an obstacle, so that one becomes one who breaks his promise and whose words prove false. Moses, upon him be peace, said: ﴿You will find me, if Allah wills, patient﴾ [al-Kahf: 70]. He was not patient, yet he was not a liar, because the exception (istithna', the qualifying phrase "if Allah wills") was present in his speech.

The second: submission to the power of Allah, the Exalted, and the acknowledgment that a person manages his actions only through the help and power of Allah.

(p-299) The third: it applies specifically to one's oath, if one swears, namely that the expiation (kaffarah) is dropped from him if he breaks it.

﴿And remember your Lord when you forget﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: when you forget something, remember Allah so that He reminds you of it. If you do so, then He has intended from you what He has reminded you of; otherwise He will guide you to what is more upright for you than what you forgot. This was said by some of the theologians (mutakallimun).

The second: "And remember your Lord when you are angry," said by Ikrimah, so that anger may leave you at the mention of Him.

The third: "And remember your Lord when you forget the exception (istithna') with the will of Allah in your oath."

Regarding the remembrance that is commanded, there are two views. The first: it is what He mentioned in the rest of the verse: ﴿And say, "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to what is nearer than this in right direction."﴾ The second: it is the statement "If Allah wills," which he had forgotten at the time of his oath.

They differed over whether the exception (istithna') is valid when made after the oath, in five opinions. The first: the exception is valid with it up to a year, so that it has the same effect as an exception made together with the oath in dropping the expiation, but it is not valid after a year. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: the exception is valid with it within the session of one's oath, but not after one has separated from it. This was said by al-Hasan and Ata.

The third: the exception is valid with it so long as one has not begun speaking something else.

The fourth: the exception is valid with it if the time is near, but not if the time is far.

The fifth: the exception is not valid with it unless it is connected to the oath. This is the apparent position of the school of Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on them both.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verse 25–26:

(p-300) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine﴾. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud it is: "They said, they remained in their cave."

On this there are two views. The first: this is the statement of the Jews, and it was said that rather it is the Christians of Najran who said that they remained in their cave three hundred years and added nine. So God, exalted is He, rejected their statement and said to His Prophet: ﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾. The second view: this is a report from God, exalted is He, of this number as the duration of their stay in the cave from the time they entered it until the time they died there.

﴿And added nine﴾ is the difference between the solar years and the lunar years.

﴿Say: God knows best how long they remained﴾. On this there are two interpretations. The first: [God knows] how long they remained after their period, until the revelation of the Qur'an concerning them. The second: God knows best how long they remained in the cave, which is the period He mentioned from the Jews, when they mentioned an addition and a subtraction.

His saying, exalted and mighty is He: ﴿How clearly He sees and hears﴾. On this there are two interpretations. The first: God sees and hears most clearly, meaning He sees best what is said and hears best what is said. The second: its meaning is that He sees them and hears them best, in what He says about them.

﴿They have no protector other than Him﴾. On this there are two interpretations. The first: no helper. The second: no preventer.

﴿And He does not make anyone a partner in His judgment﴾. On this there are two interpretations. The first: He does not make anyone a partner in the knowledge of His unseen. The second: He has not made it possible for anyone to judge by other than His judgment, so that he would become a partner to Him in His judgment.

(p-301) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you will not find, besides Him, any refuge (multaḥad)﴾. Concerning it there are four interpretations. The first: a place of refuge (malja'), said by Mujahid. The poet said:

Do not conceal from us, our brother, your affection, for among the peoples we have no multaḥad other than you.

The second: a place of escape (mahraban), said by Qutrub. The poet said:

Alas for my soul, and alas that is not of any benefit to me, and there is no escaping (multaḥad) from the decree of God.

The third: a place of deviation (ma'dilan), said by al-Akhfash.

The fourth: a protector (waliyyan), said by Qatada.

And their meanings are close to one another.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And keep yourself patient along with those who call upon their Lord﴾. Concerning it there are two interpretations. The first: they seek His exaltation (ta'zim). The second: they seek His obedience (ta'ah).

Qatada said: this verse was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ in Medina, and when it was revealed to him he said: "Praise be to God who placed among my community those with whom I have been commanded to be patient." ﴿Who call upon their Lord morning and evening﴾. Concerning it there are three interpretations. The first: they call upon Him out of desire and fear.

The second: they are those who keep to the congregational prayer, said by al-Hasan.

The third: it refers to the obligatory prayers, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

It may also bear a fourth interpretation: that it means supplication at the beginning and end of the day, so that they open their day with supplication, desiring success, and close it with supplication, seeking forgiveness.

﴿They desire His Face﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: by their supplication. The second: by the deeds of their day.

He singled out the day for this, rather than the night, because if the deeds of the day are for God, Most High, then the deeds of the night are more fitting to be for Him.

﴿And let not your eyes turn away from them﴾. Concerning it there are two interpretations:

(p-302) The first: do not let your gaze pass beyond them to others among the people of this world seeking its adornment; this was related by al-Yazidi.

The second: what Ibn Jurayj related, that 'Uyayna ibn Hisn said to the Prophet ﷺ before he embraced Islam: "The smell of Salman al-Farisi and his companions has harmed me, so make for us a gathering with you where they do not mix with us, and make for them a gathering where we do not mix with them." So this verse was revealed.

﴿And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire, and whose affair is ever excess (furuṭan)﴾. Concerning His saying ﴿made heedless (aghfalnā)﴾ there are two interpretations: The first: We made him heedless of Our remembrance. The second: We found him heedless of Our remembrance.

Concerning this heedlessness for the people of the inner thoughts (aṣḥāb al-khawāṭir) there are three aspects: The first: that it is the squandering of time through idleness, said by Sahl ibn 'Abd Allah. The second: that it is prolonged hope. The third: that it is whatever produces heedlessness.

﴿Who follows his desire﴾ has two interpretations: The first: in his appetites and his actions. The second: in his request and his seeking to be distinguished from others.

﴿And whose affair is ever furuṭan﴾ has five interpretations: The first: constriction, which is the saying of Mujahid. The second: abandoned, said by al-Farra'. The third: regret, said by Ibn Qutayba. The fourth: extravagance and excess, said by Muqatil. The fifth: swift, said by Ibn Bahr.

It is said: afrata means he exceeded (asrafa), and farraṭa means he fell short (qaṣṣara).

The second: "Whoever wills Paradise, let him believe; and whoever wills the Fire, let him disbelieve." This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: "Whoever wills, let him expose himself to Paradise through faith, and whoever wills, let him expose himself to the Fire through disbelief."

﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose enclosure surrounds them.﴾ Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: its enclosure (surradiq) is a wall of Fire encircling them; this was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is its smoke and its blaze before they reach it, and this is what God, exalted is He, referred to when He said ﴿toward a shade of three branches, neither shading nor availing against the blaze﴾ [al-Mursalat: 30–31]. This was said by Qatadah.

The third: that it is the sea that surrounds the world.

Yaʿla ibn Umayyah narrated, saying: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "The sea is Jahannam," and then he recited ﴿a Fire whose enclosure surrounds them﴾, and then said: "By God, I will never enter it as long as I live, and not a drop of it will touch me." The word surradiq (enclosure) is a Persian word that has been Arabicized, and its origin is surradar.

﴿And if they seek relief, they will be relieved with water like molten metal (al-muhl)﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations. The first: it is pus and blood; this was said by Mujahid.

The third: it is everything that has been melted until it has liquefied; this was said by Ibn Masʿud.

The fourth: it is that whose heat has reached its extreme; this was said by Saʿid ibn Jubayr. The poet said:

"It was mixed with water from it, a loathsome molten metal; then it was poured over the backs after the drinking."

He considered this to be relief (ighathah) because it is paired with the mention of seeking relief.

﴿Evil is the drink, and evil is the resting-place (murtafaq).﴾ Regarding murtafaq there are four interpretations. The first: its meaning is "a place of gathering," this was said by Mujahid, as though he took it to mean companionship (murafaqah).

(p-304) The second: "a dwelling," this was said by al-Kalbi, derived from irtifaq (reclining/resting).

The third: that it is from rifq (kindness, gentleness).

The fourth: that it is from the couch (mutaka'), with the meaning of "resting on the elbow" (mirfaq), and from this is the saying of Abu Dhu'ayb:

"The one at ease slept, while I spent the night reclining on my elbow, as though my eyes had in them aloe-poison that has been slaughtered."

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, indeed We do not waste the reward of one who does good work.﴾ al-Bara' ibn 'Azib narrated that "a Bedouin stood before the Messenger of Allah ﷺ during the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada') and said: 'I am a man who seeks knowledge, so inform me about this verse, ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds﴾ to the end of the verse.'

The Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, said: '(O Bedouin, you are not far from them, nor are they far from you. They are these four who are standing: Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali. So inform your people that this verse was revealed concerning them.)'"

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿and they will wear green garments of fine silk (sundus) and brocade (istabraq)﴾. As for sundus, there are two opinions. One is that it is the finest of brocade (dibaj), said by al-Kalbi. The second is that it is the thinnest of brocade, its singular being sundusah, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

(p-305)

Sometimes you see them wearing the mashair (cloaks),
and at other times, istabraq brocade is their garment.

The second opinion is that it is silk woven with gold, said by Ibn Bahr.

The second is that they are the furnishings within the hijal. The third is that they are the thrones within the hijal. The poet has said:

Cheeks that were worn down by the journey, until it is as if
they were touching the soft cloth (al-ma'za') with the touch of couches.

One is that it is the finest of brocade (dibaj), said by al-Kalbi. The second is that it is the thinnest of brocade, its singular being sundusah, said by Ibn Qutaybah.

As for istabraq, there are two opinions. One is that it is the thickest of brocade, said by Ibn Qutaybah. It is a Persian word that has been Arabized, its origin being istabrah, meaning "the strong," and al-Muraqqish has said:

(p-305)

Sometimes you see them wearing the mashair (cloaks),
and at other times, istabraq brocade is their garment.

The second opinion is that it is silk woven with gold, said by Ibn Bahr.

﴿Reclining therein upon the arā'ik (couches)﴾. Concerning arā'ik there are three opinions. The first is that they are the hijal (canopied enclosures), said by al-Zajjaj. Cheeks that were worn down by the journey, until it is as if
they were touching the soft cloth (al-ma'za') with the touch of couches.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 32–36:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And set forth for them the parable of two men: We granted one of them two gardens﴾. Al-jannah is al-bustan (the orchard). When it combines grapevines and palm trees, with crops beneath them, it is the most beautiful of gardens and the most beneficial, because of the fruit of its upper part and the crops of its lower part. This is the meaning of His saying ﴿And We placed between them a field of crops﴾. ﴿Both gardens yielded their produce﴾, meaning their fruit and their crops. He called it ukul (produce) because it is eaten.

﴿And had not failed in aught therefrom﴾, meaning that it yielded all of its fruit and crops in full.

﴿And We caused a river to gush forth between them﴾, meaning that there were streams of water within them, so their fruit and crops were more abundant and better watered through the continuous flow of water. This is the utmost of the qualities in what yields benefit and increase.

Regarding the setting forth of this parable of the two gardens, there are two opinions. The first is what Muqatil ibn Sulayman related: that it is God's report, may He be exalted, concerning two brothers among the Children of Israel who inherited a large amount of wealth from their father. Ibn Abbas said it was eight thousand dinars.

One of them took his share while he was a believer, and he drew near to God, the Exalted, with it. The other took his share while he was a disbeliever, and with it he acquired estates, among them these two gardens, and he did not draw near to God, the Exalted, with any of it. What befell him was what God mentioned afterward. God made him a parable for this community.

The second opinion is that it is a parable which God, the Exalted, set forth for this community, and it is not a report about a past situation, in order to make them abstain from the world and desire the Hereafter. He made it a rebuke and a warning.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And he had fruit﴾. Asim read thamarun with a fatha on the tha and the mim. Abu Amr read it with a damma on the tha and a sukun on the mim. The rest read thumurun with a damma on both the tha and the mim.

Regarding the difference between these two readings (qira'at, the recognized variant recitations) with damma and with fatha, there are two opinions. The first is that their meaning is one and the same. On this view there are three interpretations (ta'wil, explanation of meaning). The first: it is gold and silver, said by Qatadah, because they are fruitful wealth. The second: it is abundant wealth of various kinds, said by Ibn Abbas, because its multiplication is greater. The third: it is the principal that has growth, said by Ibn Zayd, because growth involves multiplication.

The second opinion is that the meanings of the damma and fatha readings differ. On this view there are four aspects to distinguishing them. The first: with fatha it is the plural of thamarah (a single fruit), and with damma it is the plural of thimar (fruits).

The second: with fatha it refers specifically to date-palm fruit, and with damma it refers to all wealth. This was said by Ibn Bahr.

The third: with fatha it is what its fruit comes from its own root, and with damma it is what its fruit comes from something other than itself.

The fourth: thamar with damma is the root, and with fatha it is the branch. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

Regarding this mentioned fruit, there are two opinions. The first: it is the fruit of the two gardens mentioned earlier. This is the view of the majority.

The second: it is fruit he owned from outside his two gardens, whose root had belonged to someone else, just as people own fruits without owning their roots. This was said by Ibn Abbas, so that in his ownership would be gathered the fruit of his own property and the fruit of property not his own, making his ownership more general.

﴿He said to his companion﴾, meaning to his Muslim brother, who had spent his wealth on acts of devotion, seeking reward in the Hereafter, while this disbeliever spent his wealth on what he kept for the world and for multiplying his possessions.

(p-307) ﴿And he was disputing with him﴾, meaning he was debating with him. Regarding what he disputed with him, there are two aspects. The first: concerning faith and disbelief. The second: concerning the pursuit of the world and the pursuit of the Hereafter. So there took place between them what God, the Exalted, related of their words.

**Al-Mawardi, *al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*, on verses 37–41 of Surah al-Kahf**

﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: something better than your garden in this world, so that I would be equal to you in it.

The second, which is the more well-known: something better than your garden in the Hereafter, so that I would be superior to you in it.

﴿And send upon it a calamity from the sky﴾. In this there are five interpretations. The first: it means a punishment ('adhab). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada.

The second: fire.

The third: locusts.

The fourth: a reckoning punishment (*'adhab hisab*) for what your hands have earned. This was said by al-Zajjaj, because it is the recompense of the Hereafter. And recompense from Allah the Exalted is by reckoning (*bi-hisab*).

The fifth: that it refers to the many projectiles (*al-marami al-kathira*). This was said by al-Akhfash, and its root meaning is *al-hisab*, which are the arrows shot in one volley, and this was from the shooting of the Asawira (Persian cavalrymen).

﴿So it becomes a barren, slippery ground﴾: meaning a bare white land on which no plant grows and on which no foot can stand firm. It becomes the most harmful land, after having been a garden, the most beneficial land.

﴿Or its water sinks away into the earth﴾: meaning its water becomes *ghawran*, that is, sunken and gone. Here *aw* (or) is placed in the position of *waw* (and), and *ghawran* means sinking and disappearing, so that it becomes the land most devoid of water, after having had water in it.

(p-308) ﴿Then you will not be able to seek it﴾. It may carry two meanings. The first: you will not be able to bring back the sunken water. The second: you will not be able to seek anything else in its place.

With this limit the debate with his companion and his warning came to an end.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 18, verses 42–44:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed (by ruin)﴾, meaning his wealth was destroyed. This was the first way in which God fulfilled the warning of his brother.

﴿So he began to wring his hands over what he had spent on it﴾. This admits of two interpretations. The first: he wrung his hands in regret over what he had spent on it and in grief over what was lost.

The second: he turned over his property, finding in it no return for what he had spent, which was destroyed. This is because ownership (*al-milk*) is sometimes expressed by "the hand," from their saying: "there is wealth in his hand," meaning in his possession.

﴿And it was fallen over its trellises﴾, meaning it was overturned upon its supports. Thus he was struck with the destruction of both the root and the fruit, and this is among the greatest of calamities, as a recompense for his rebellion.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿And he had no company to help him against God﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: *al-fi'a* (company) means troops, as said by al-Kalbi (*al-Kalbi*).

The second: it means clan, as said by Mujahid (*Mujahid*).

﴿Nor was he able to defend himself﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations. The first: he was not able to protect himself, as said by Qatada (*Qatada*).

The second: he was not able to recover in place of what had been lost from him.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 45–46:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿And present to them the parable of the life of this world: it is like water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it⁠—﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: the water mingled with the plants when they became full-grown. The second: the plants mingled with one another when the water descended upon them, until they grew.

﴿Then it becomes dry stubble, scattered by the winds⁠﴾ means: when the water is withheld from it. The clause was omitted for brevity, since the discourse points to it. Al-hashim (dry stubble) is what has crumbled after drying out, from the leaves of trees and crops. The poet said:

؎ Then their bodies became *nayyiman*, which whoever saw them likened to *al-hashim* (dry stubble).

Scholars differed regarding the purpose of coining this parable, on two views. The first: Allah, Exalted, coined it as a parable for this world, to indicate its passing away after its beauty and splendor.

The second: Allah, Exalted, coined it as a parable for the conditions of the people of this world, that with every blessing there is a calamity, and with every joy there is a sorrow.

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world⁠﴾ because in wealth there is beauty and benefit, and in children there is strength and protection; thus they became the adornment of the life of this world.

﴿But the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope⁠﴾. Regarding them there are four interpretations. The first: they are the five daily prayers. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Saʿid ibn Jubayr.

The second: they are righteous deeds. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: they are good words. This is also narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, and was said by ʿAtiyyah al-ʿAwfi.

The fourth: it is the saying "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is the Greatest, and there is no power nor strength except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty." This was said by ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, may Allah be pleased with him.

Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, related that he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Glory be to Allah, praise be to Allah, there is no god but Allah, and Allah is the Greatest, these are the enduring good deeds."

Regarding ﴿righteous⁠﴾ (al-salihat) there are two meanings. The first: it means "those who are righteous" (al-salihin), because the righteous one is the doer of righteousness.

The second: it means "beneficial," so he expressed benefit by righteousness, since benefit is a source of good.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "When I was taken up to the heaven, I was shown Ibrahim (Abraham), who said: 'Command your Community to plant abundantly the trees of Paradise, for its soil is good and its land is spacious.' I said: 'And what are the trees of Paradise?' He said: 'There is no power nor strength except with Allah, the Most High, the Mighty.'"

﴿better with your Lord in reward⁠﴾ means in the Hereafter, and ﴿better in hope⁠﴾ means in your own estimation in this world. The meaning of His saying ﴿better in hope⁠﴾ is: more truthful in hope, because among hopes there are false ones, whereas this hope does not deceive.

"And [mention] the Day We set the mountains in motion, and you see the earth laid bare, and We gather them and leave not one of them behind." Concerning the phrase ﴿And the Day We set the mountains in motion﴾ there are three interpretations. The first: We set them moving (from sayr, "motion"), until they are removed from their places, because of the manifest sign in this and the great lesson in it. The second: We set them moving, meaning We reduce them, until what was great of them becomes small and slight. The third: that He makes them scattered dust (haba'an manthuran).

﴿And you see the earth laid bare﴾ concerning this there are two views. The first: that it is the bringing forth of what is in its belly of the dead, by their coming out of their graves. The second: that it is a flat plain, not covered by any mountain or vegetation.

﴿And We gather them, and leave not one of them behind﴾ concerning this there are three interpretations.

The first: meaning We leave none of them behind; this is said by Ibn Qutaybah, who said that from this the pool (ghadir) was named, because it is what the floods leave behind (tukhallifuhu). 

The second: We do not make anyone of them a successor (istikhlaf); this is said by al-Kalbi.

The third: its meaning is that We do not leave any of them; this is related by Muqatil.

﴿And they are presented before your Lord in rows﴾ It is said that they will be presented row after row, like the rows in prayer. It is also said that they will be gathered naked, barefoot and uncircumcised. ʿĀ'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, said: "Then will they not be ashamed on that day?" The second: that the reckoning is placed; this is said by al-Kalbi, and the reckoning is expressed by "the Book" because they will be reckoned for their recorded deeds.

﴿So you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾ because Allah has counted it and they have forgotten it.

﴿And they will say, "Woe to us! What is this Book that leaves nothing small or great but has counted it!"﴾ Concerning "small" there are two interpretations. It may also bear a third view: that the "small" is desire and the "great" is action.

﴿And they will find what they did present﴾ this may bear two interpretations. The first: they will find the counting of what they did present in the Book. The second: they will find the recompense for what they did, immediate, on the Day of Resurrection.

﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ meaning: none of the obedient is deprived of any part of his reward, nor is any disobedient one given an increase in his punishment.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verse 50:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," so they prostrated, except Iblis. He was of the jinn⦆ There are three opinions regarding this.

The first: he was of the jinn, as Allah Most High has mentioned.

The one who holds this view then rejected that he was of the angels, for two reasons. The first: he has offspring (dhurriyyah), and the angels have no offspring.

The second: the angels are the messengers of Allah, glorified is He, and disbelief is not permissible for them, whereas Iblis did disbelieve. Al-Hasan said: "Iblis was never of the angels for even the blink of an eye, and he is indeed the origin of the jinn, just as Adam is the origin of mankind."

The second opinion: he was of the angels. Those who held this view differed over the meaning of the words of Allah Most High, ﴿he was of the jinn⦆, according to three opinions.

The first: what Qatadah said, that he was of the noblest category of angels called the jinn.

The second: what Ibn Abbas said, that he was among the angels, from the guardians of Paradise and the managers of the affairs of the lowest heaven; therefore he was called "of the jinn" in reference to the guardians of Paradise, just as one says "Makki" and "Basri" (of Mecca and of Basra).

The third: that the jinn are a tribe of the angels, created from fire, and Iblis was among them, while the rest of the angels were created from light. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Al-Hasan also said: Iblis was created from fire and to fire he will return.

The third opinion: Iblis was neither of mankind nor of the jinn, but was of the jann (a kind of hidden being). His name and the derivation of it have already been mentioned sufficiently.

﴿So he defied the command of his Lord⦆ There are two interpretations regarding this. The first: fisq means expansion, and its meaning is that he expanded in the prohibitions of Allah Most High.

The second: fisq means exit, i.e., he went out from the obedience of his Lord, from the expression "fasaqat al-rutbah" when the date (rutab) came out of its skin. The rat was named fuwaysiqah because it comes out of its hole. Ru'bah ibn al-Ajjaj said:

They plunge from Najd and from a deep valley, departing (fawasiq) from their path, deviating (jawa'ir).

And regarding His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers⦆ there are two interpretations. The first: how evil is what they substituted for obedience to Allah with obedience to Iblis; this was said by Qatadah.

The second: how evil is what they substituted for Paradise with the Fire.

(p-315) His words, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿I did not make them witness the creation of the heavens and the earth﴾ has two interpretations. The first: I did not make Iblis and his offspring witness it. The second: I did not make all of creation witness the creation of the heavens and the earth.

Also in it are two interpretations. The first: I did not make them witness it seeking their help in creating it. The second: I did not make them witness its creation so that they would know of My power, which would prevent them from disbelieving.

It may also bear a third meaning: I did not make them witness its creation so that they would encompass knowledge of its unseen, since Allah is singled out with knowledge of the unseen, not His creation.

﴿Nor the creation of themselves﴾ has two interpretations. The first: I did not seek help from some of them in creating others. The second: I did not make some of them witness the creation of others.

It may also bear a third meaning: I did not inform them of the creation of themselves, so how would they know the creation of others?

﴿And I would not have taken misleaders as helpers﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: it means allies (awliya'). The second: it means helpers (a'wan). I found this transmitted from al-Kalbi.

As for what is meant by not taking them as helpers, there are two interpretations. The first: helpers in creating the heavens and the earth. The second: helpers for the worshippers of idols, as said by al-Kalbi.

(p-316) Regarding these misleaders, there are two opinions. The first: Iblis and his offspring. The second: every misleader among all creatures.

Some of the early generations (al-salaf) said: If a person's sin stems from desire, then hope for him; but if it stems from arrogance, then do not hope for him. Iblis's sin stemmed from arrogance, so his repentance was not accepted, whereas Adam's sin stemmed from desire, so Allah accepted his repentance.

Some poets have alluded to this meaning, saying:

When the youth falls into his error, then call the youth back to piety, and summon him to it.
For the caravan may stray from the path of the road, then return to its course.

**The word of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And We placed between them a "mawbiq" (a place of ruin)﴾.** Regarding it there are six opinions. The first: a "majlis" (gathering place), said by al-Rabi'.

The second: a place of destruction, said by Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada and al-Dahhak. A poet said:

*I seek forgiveness from God for my deeds that have passed,*
*for a slip, for which if You hold me to account, I would be destroyed.*

That is, I would be ruined. Similar is the saying of Zuhayr:

*Whoever buys a good reputation with his wealth,*
*protects his honour from every shameful, ruinous thing.*

Al-Farra' said: He made their connection in this world a ruin for them in the Hereafter.

The third: a promised place (of meeting), said by Abu 'Ubayda.

The fourth: enmity, said by al-Hasan.

The fifth: that it is a valley in Hell, said by Anas ibn Malik.

(p-317) The sixth: that it is a valley separating Paradise and the Fire, related by some of the later scholars.

**The word of the Exalted and Majestic: ﴿And the criminals saw the Fire﴾.** This may carry two meanings. The first: they witnessed it at the place of gathering. The second: they knew of it at the time of the presentation (before God).

**﴿So they thought that they were going to fall into it﴾.** Regarding this there are two meanings. The first: they hoped for pardon before entering it, and therefore they thought that they would fall into it. The second: they knew for certain that they would fall into it, because they had come into the abode of certainty, and knowledge is sometimes expressed by "thought" (ẓann), because thought is the precursor of knowledge.

**﴿And they will not find from it any escape﴾.** Regarding this there are two meanings. The first: "maṣraf" means a refuge, said by al-Kalbi. The second: a place of turning to which they might turn, said by Ibn Qutayba. From this is the saying of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

*O Zuhayr, is there any escape from the grey-haired (age)?*
*Or is there no eternity for the one who spends, who strains (himself)?*

Regarding what is intended there are two meanings. The first: the polytheists did not find an escape from the Fire. The second: the idols did not find a way to turn the Fire away from the polytheists.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verse 54:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an for the people from every example﴾ admits of two meanings. One of them: what He mentioned to them of lessons from the earlier generations.

The second: what He made clear to them of the proofs of Lordship. So on the first meaning it is a recompense (jaza'), and on the second it is an explanation (bayan).

﴿But mankind has been, more than anything, contentious﴾ admits of two meanings. One of them: obstinacy (inad), which is the requirement of the first meaning.

The second: argumentation (hijaj), which is the requirement of the second saying.

It has been narrated that "the Prophet (ﷺ) entered upon Ali and Fatima, may Allah be pleased with them both, while they were sleeping, and said: (Prayer! Will you not pray?) Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, said: Indeed our souls are in the hand of Allah; when He wills to raise them, He raises them. So the Prophet (ﷺ) turned away while saying ﴿But mankind has been, more than anything, contentious﴾ [al-Kahf: 54]."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 55–56:

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿And what prevented the people from believing when the guidance had come to them﴾. In this there are two interpretations. The first: "And what prevented the people themselves from believing." The second: "What prevented the Satan from [preventing] the people from believing."

And in "the guidance" there are two interpretations. The first: the proofs of Allah that indicate His oneness and the obligation of obeying Him. The second: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, sent for the guidance of creation.

﴿Except that there come upon them the way of the earlier peoples﴾, i.e., the custom of the earlier peoples in the punishment of annihilation.

﴿Or that the punishment come upon them face to face﴾. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī read ﴿qubulan﴾ with a ḍammah on the qāf and the bāʾ. In it there are two interpretations. The first: "confrontation," as said by Mujāhid.

The second: that it is the plural of qabīl, meaning "kinds of punishment."

And it may admit a third meaning: that He intends "from before them, facing them," so that the terror of witnessing it becomes severe upon them.

The rest of the readers read ﴿qibalan﴾ with a kasrah on the qāf. In it there are two interpretations. The first: "in front of [them]."

The second: "by direct observation."

And it may admit a third meaning: "from the side of Allah, exalted, with a punishment from the sky, not from the side of created beings," because it encompasses and leaves nothing, so it is more severe and greater.

His saying, exalted and majestic is He: ﴿That they may refute by it the truth﴾. In it there are three interpretations. The first: "that they may take away the truth by it and remove it," as said by al-Akhfash.

The second: "that they may nullify the Qur'an by it and alter it," as said by al-Kalbī.

The third: "that they may destroy the truth by it."

The word *dāḥiḍ* means "perishing," derived from *al-daḥḍ*, which is the slippery place on the earth on which no hoof, hoof-shaped foot, or foot can stand firm. The poet said:

I perished, and his caution saved the Yashkurī, and he swerved as a camel swerves from the slippery ground.

﴿And they take My signs and what they are warned of in mockery﴾. It may admit two interpretations. The first: that "the signs" are the proof, and "what they are warned of" is the Qur'an. The second: "the signs" are the Qur'an, and "what they are warned of" is the people.

And His saying ﴿in mockery﴾ may admit two interpretations. The first: "in play." The second: "in falsehood."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verse 57–59:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your Lord is the Forgiving﴾, meaning, of sins. This belongs specifically to the people of faith, not to the disbelievers.

﴿Full of mercy﴾. On this there are four interpretations. The first: possessor of pardon.

The second: possessor of reward. On these two interpretations it belongs specifically to the people of faith, not to the disbelievers.

The third: possessor of blessing.

The fourth: possessor of guidance. On these two interpretations it encompasses both the people of faith and the people of disbelief, because He bestows blessings in this world upon the disbeliever just as He bestows them upon the believer, and He has made His guidance clear to the disbeliever just as He made it clear to the believer, even though only the believer is guided by it and not the disbeliever.

﴿Rather, for them there is an appointed promise﴾. On this there are two interpretations. One: a predetermined term to which they are deferred.

The second: a due recompense for which they will be called to account.

﴿They will never find besides Him a refuge﴾. On this there are four interpretations. The first: a shelter, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Zayd.

The second: a place of safety, said by Mujahid.

The third: a protector, said by Qatadah.

The fourth: a place of escape, said by Abu 'Ubaydah.

He said: The Arabs say: "Lā wa'alat nafsuhu," meaning, "May he not escape," and from it is the saying of the poet:

Lā wa'alat nafsuka, you let it go to the Amiris and it was not wounded (lit. "was not wounded/hurt").

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those towns — We destroyed them when they wronged﴾. On this there are two interpretations:

(p-321) The first: We destroyed them with punishment when they wronged through disbelief.

The second: We destroyed them by leaving them to the consequences of their own poor management when they wronged through abandoning gratitude.

﴿And We appointed for their destruction an appointed time﴾. On this there are two interpretations. The first: a term to which they are deferred, said by Mujahid.

The second: a time in which they would be destroyed.

It is recited with a ḍammah and with a fatḥah on the mīm: with a ḍammah it is from ahlaka (to destroy), and with a fatḥah it is from halaka (to perish).

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah al-Kahf, verses 60–65:

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Musa said to his servant﴾. He means Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun), who was the son of Musa's sister. He was called his "fata" (servant/attendant) because he constantly accompanied him. It is said that this was in knowledge, and it is said that it was in service. He was Musa's successor over his people after him.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The Musa who sought al-Khidr was Musa ibn Munashsha ibn Yusuf, and he was a prophet among the Children of Israel before Musa ibn Imran.

What the majority of Muslims hold is that he was Musa ibn Imran.

[p-322] ﴿I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: it means the Sea of Rome and the Sea of Persia, one of them towards the east and the other towards the west. al-Tabari related that there is no place on earth with more water than it.

The second opinion: it is the sea of Armenia, on the side of the Gates (al-Abwab).

The third: it refers to al-Khidr and Ilyas, who are two seas of knowledge. This is related from al-Suddi.

﴿Or I will continue for a long period (huqub)﴾. Concerning this there are five views. The first: a huqub is eighty years, as said by Abdullah ibn Umar.

The second: seventy years, as said by Mujahid.

The third: that a huqub is a time period, as said by Qatadah.

The fourth: that it is an age (al-dahr), as said by Ibn Abbas, and from it is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"We are the kings and the sons of kings, and for us is a kingdom by which these people have lived for ages."

The fifth: that it means a year in the dialect of Qays, as said by al-Kalbi.

Concerning his words ﴿I will not cease (la abrah)﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: "I will not part from you," and from it is the poet's saying:

"If you do not cease (tabrah) to discharge a trust, and another trust that has burdened you with its weight remains."

[p-323] The second: "I will not stop," as said by al-Farra'; and from it is the poet's saying:

"And I will not cease, as long as God keeps my people, by the praise of God, girded and commendable."

That is, I will not stop.

It is said that he said ﴿I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾ because he had been promised that he would meet al-Khidr, peace be upon him, there.

﴿So when they reached the meeting place between them, they forgot their fish﴾. It is said that they had taken a salted fish as provision, and they left it when they sat down. Concerning this there are two views. The first: it escaped from them until it took its path into the sea by a tunnel, so their losing track of it was called forgetting on their part.

The second: it is from forgetting it and neglecting it.

Then there are two views. The first: the one who forgot it was only one of them, Yusha' ibn Nun, although the forgetting is attributed to both of them, as one says "the people forgot their provisions" when one of them forgot.

The second: Yusha' forgot to carry the fish, and Musa forgot to instruct him about it, so each of them was forgetful of something different from what the other had forgotten.

﴿And it took its path into the sea, going freely﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: a way (maslakan), as said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The second: dry (yabsan), as said by al-Kalbi.

The third: a marvel ('ajaban), as said by Muqatil.

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿So when they had passed on﴾, meaning, past the place of the fish.

﴿He said to his servant﴾, meaning Musa said to his servant Yusha' ibn Nun.

﴿Bring us our morning meal﴾. Al-ghada' is the food of the morning (al-ghadah), just as al-'asha' is the food of the evening, and a person has more need of the morning meal than of the evening meal.

﴿Indeed we have suffered from this journey of ours exhaustion (nasab)﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: it is fatigue. The second: weakness.

[p-324] ﴿He said: "Did you see when we took refuge at the rock?"﴾. Concerning this there are two statements. The first: as said by Muqatil, the rock is in a land called Sharwan on the shore of the Sea of Ayla, and beside it is a spring called the Spring of Life.

The second: it is the rock that lies beyond the river of Zayt on the road.

﴿Indeed I forgot the fish﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: indeed I forgot to carry the fish. The second: indeed I forgot to inform you of the matter of the fish.

﴿And none made me forget it except Satan, that I should mention it﴾, meaning, he made me forget it by his whisperings to me and by occupying my heart.

﴿And it took its path into the sea in a marvelous way﴾. Concerning this there are two statements. The first: it used to be that whenever it took a path in the sea, the water would turn into stone, so when Musa saw this he marvelled at the water becoming stone.

The second: it is the rock that lies beyond the river of Zayt on the road.

﴿Indeed I forgot the fish﴾. Concerning this there are two views. The first: indeed I forgot to carry the fish. The second: indeed I forgot to inform you of the matter of the fish.

﴿And none made me forget it except Satan, that I should mention it﴾, meaning, he made me forget it by his whisperings to me and by occupying my heart.

﴿And it took its path into the sea in a marvelous way﴾. Concerning this there are two statements. The first: it used to be that whenever it took a path in the sea, the water would turn into stone, so when Musa saw this he marvelled at the water becoming stone.

The second: when Yusha' informed Musa of the matter of the fish, Musa returned to its place and saw the trace of the fish in the sea and its circular track along which it had moved, and he marvelled at the fish's return to life.

﴿So they returned, retracing their footsteps (qasasan)﴾, meaning they went back along their tracks, following the trace of the fish and pursuing it.

﴿And they found a servant from among Our servants, whom We had given mercy from Us﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations. The first: prophethood, as said by Muqatil. The second: blessing. The third: obedience. The fourth: long life.

The commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah al-Kahf, verses 60–65:

His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And when Musa said to his servant﴾. He means Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun), who was the son of Musa's sister. He was called his "fata" (servant/attendant) because he constantly accompanied him. It is said that this was in knowledge, and it is said that it was in service. He was Musa's successor over his people after him.

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: The Musa who sought al-Khidr was Musa ibn Munashsha ibn Yusuf, and he was a prophet among the Children of Israel before Musa ibn Imran.

What the majority of Muslims hold is that he was Musa ibn Imran.

The first: it means the Sea of Rome and the Sea of Persia, one of them towards the east and the other towards the west. al-Tabari related that there is no place on earth with more water than it.

The second opinion: it is the sea of Armenia, on the side of the Gates (al-Abwab).

The third: it refers to al-Khidr and Ilyas, who are two seas of knowledge. This is related from al-Suddi.

﴿Or I will continue for a long period (huqub)﴾. Concerning this there are five views. The first: a huqub is eighty years, as said by Abdullah ibn Umar.

The second: seventy years, as said by Mujahid.

The third: that a huqub is a time period, as said by Qatadah.

The fourth: that it is an age (al-dahr), as said by Ibn Abbas, and from it is the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

"We are the kings and the sons of kings, and for us is a kingdom by which these people have lived for ages."

The fifth: that it means a year in the dialect of Qays, as said by al-Kalbi.

Concerning his words ﴿I will not cease (la abrah)﴾ there are two interpretations. The first: "I will not part from you," and from it is the poet's saying:

"If you do not cease (tabrah) to discharge a trust, and another trust that has burdened you with its weight remains."

[p-323] The second: "I will not stop," as said by al-Farra'; and from it is the poet's saying:

"And I will not cease, as long as God keeps my people, by the praise of God, girded and commendable."

That is, I will not stop.

It is said that he said ﴿I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas﴾ because he had been promised that he would meet al-Khidr, peace be upon him, there.

Concerning this there are two views. The first: it escaped from them until it took its path into the sea by a tunnel, so their losing track of it was called forgetting on their part.

The second: it is from forgetting it and neglecting it.

Then there are two views. The first: the one who forgot it was only one of them, Yusha' ibn Nun, although the forgetting is attributed to both of them, as one says "the people forgot their provisions" when one of them forgot.

The second: Yusha' forgot to carry the fish, and Musa forgot to instruct him about it, so each of them was forgetful of something different from what the other had forgotten.

The second: dry (yabsan), as said by al-Kalbi.

The third: a marvel ('ajaban), as said by Muqatil.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 66–70:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying: ﴿Moses said to him, "May I follow you on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, [that which is] right guidance?"﴾ Concerning "right guidance" (rushd) here there are three interpretations. The first: it means knowledge. This is the view of Muqatil, and its sense would be: "on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught, knowledge."

The second: its meaning is "on condition that you teach me of what you have been taught by God's guidance to you."

The third: [it means] what he (al-Khidr) sees in the knowledge of al-Khidr as right conduct which he does, and error (ghayy) which he avoids. So Moses asked him to teach him of the right conduct which he practises, and did not ask him to teach him the error which he avoids, because he already knew the error which he avoids but did not know that right conduct.

﴿He said, "Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me.﴾ It admits of two meanings. The first: patience regarding questioning.

The second: patience regarding disapproval (inkar).

﴿And how can you have patience over that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾ Concerning this there are two meanings. The first: you have not found a cause for it.

The second: you have not known its knowledge, because al-Khidr knew that Moses would not be patient when he saw what outwardly appears objectionable.
