The Exalted said: ﴿So they set out, until when they boarded the ship, he made a hole in it.﴾ This was because he intended to cross the sea to another land. He boarded the ship while it carried passengers. Al-Khadir took an axe and a chisel and made a hole in the ship until water entered it. It is said that he pulled two planks out of it, and its passengers cried out from fear of drowning.

Then Musa said to him: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people?﴾ Although the sinking of the ship would have meant the drowning of all of them, he was more concerned for the people than for himself, because this is the habit of the Prophets.

Then, after his astonishment and his great disapproval, he said: ﴿You have certainly done a dreadful thing (shay'an imra).﴾ He first magnified the matter and then denounced it. There are three interpretations of the word imr:

First: it means an abominable thing (munkaran). This was said by Mujahid.

Second: it means a marvel (ajaban). This was said by Muqatil.

Third: that imr means a great calamity (al-dahiya al-'azima). This was said by Abu 'Ubayda, who recited:

"The rivals have met from me a denounced, calamitous disaster, a great and dreadful affair (imra)."

The word is derived from al-imr, meaning what is corrupt and needs to be set right. From it comes the phrase rajul imr, meaning a man of weak judgement, because he needs to be commanded until his judgement becomes strong. From it also comes amira al-qawm, meaning the people became numerous, because they need someone to command and forbid them.

The Exalted said: ﴿He said, "Do not hold me accountable for what I forgot."﴾ On this there are three interpretations:

First: "for what I forgot and was heedless of, so I did not remember it." Ubayy ibn Ka'b traced this back to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a marfu' report.

Second: "for what I seemingly forgot, though in reality I did not forget it." Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn Abbas that he said: "He did not forget, but these are ma'arid al-kalam (indirect or allusive expressions)."

Third: "for what I abandoned of your covenant." This was said by Ibn Abbas. It is derived from nisyan in the sense of abandonment (al-tark), not from nisyan in the sense of inadvertence (al-sahw).

﴿And do not burden me with difficulty in my affair.﴾ On this there are four interpretations:

First: "Do not rebuke me for what I abandoned of your instruction." This was said by al-Dahhak.

Second: "Let not hardship overtake me from you." This comes from the expression ghulam murahiq, meaning a boy who is near to reaching puberty (yaghshahu al-bulugh). From this is the hadith of 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Irhaqu al-qibla," meaning, approach the qibla and come close to it.

Third: "Do not burden me with what I am not able to do, namely guarding myself against error and forgetting." This is the meaning of Muqatil's statement.

Fourth: "Let not my dismissal from you overtake me."

The Exalted said: ﴿So they set out, until when they met a boy, and he killed him.﴾ This means that Musa and al-Khadir set out. It is possible that Yusha' lagged behind them, since what is mentioned is the departure of two. This is the more apparent view, because Musa was specially chosen for prophethood and his meeting with al-Khadir was by revelation. It is also possible that he was with them but was not mentioned, because he was a follower of Musa. The one who is followed was mentioned without the follower, and Musa's words ﴿That is what we were seeking﴾ were a reference to his servant Yusha'.

There is disagreement about whether the slain boy had reached puberty. Ibn Abbas said: he was a young man who had a beard, because one who has not reached puberty is not held accountable by the pen for an act that would make him deserve execution. The word ghulam may be applied to a man. Layla al-Akhyaliyya said about al-Hajjaj:

"He healed them from the incurable disease that was upon them, a young man (ghulam) who, when he shakes the spear, gives them drink."

Most scholars said he was young, had not reached puberty, and was playing with children, until al-Khadir passed by him and killed him.

On the reason for his killing there are two views:

First: because he was created with disbelief (kufr) in his nature.

Second: because by killing him he set right the condition of his parents.

On the manner of his killing there are two views:

First: he seized him from among the children, threw him down and slaughtered him with a knife. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Second: he took a stone and killed the boy with it. This was said by Muqatil.

Musa regarded what al-Khadir had done, the killing of the boy without a cause, as grievous, and so he said: ﴿Have you killed a pure soul without a soul (to avenge)?﴾ Scholars differ on whether he said this as a question seeking information or as a denunciation, and there are two views:

First: he said it as a question seeking information, because he knew that al-Khadir would not transgress the rights of Allah.

Second: he said it as a denunciation of him, because he had said ﴿You have certainly done a terrible thing.﴾ Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read zakiyatan (with an alif). Hamza, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim and al-Kisa'i read zakiyyatan (without an alif).

Regarding zakiyatan and zakiyyatan there are two views:

First, and this is the view of most scholars, that the two words have the same meaning. On this view, the interpretation has six possibilities:

First: that zakiya means repentant. This was said by Qatada.

Second: that it means pure. This was related by Ibn 'Isa.

Third: that it means growing and increasing. This was said by many commentators. Nabigha of Banu Dhubyan said:

"Whatever you delayed of your worldly life is no loss, and if you advanced it, zaka' (increase) will return to you."

He meant increase.

Fourth: that zakiya means a Muslim. This was said by Ibn Abbas, because in his view the slain boy was a man.

Fifth: that zakiya means one whose blood was not lawful to shed. This was said by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'.

Sixth: that zakiya means one who had not committed sins. This was said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The second view is that there is a distinction between zakiya and zakiyya, and on this there are three interpretations:

First: zakiya refers to the body (purity of the body), while zakiyya refers to religion. This is the view of Abu 'Ubayda.

Second: zakiyya is more intensive than zakiya. This was said by Tha'lab.

Third: zakiya is one who has not sinned, while zakiyya is one who sinned and then repented, so she was forgiven. This was said by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'.

﴿You have certainly done a terrible thing (shay'an nukra).﴾ On this there are four interpretations:

First: a thing that is abominable (munkaran). This was said by al-Kalbi.

Second: an affair that is shameful and ugly. This is the meaning of Muqatil's statement.

Third: it is that which must be denounced and not done.

Fourth: it is more severe than imr. This was said by Qatada.

(p-٣٣١) Regarding ﴿So they set out until, when they came to the people of a town, they asked its people for food﴾, there are three opinions about this town. The first is that it is Antioch, reported by al-Kalbi.

The second is that it is al-Ubulla, reported by Qatadah.

The third is that it is Bajirwan in Armenia, reported by Muqatil.

﴿But they refused to entertain them as guests﴾. It is said: "Adafta al-rajul" (you hosted the man) when he stays with you, so you are a host (mudif). And "wadaftu al-rajul" (you were a guest of the man) when you stay with him, so you are a guest (dayf).

The request for food from the two of them was an excuse for them. The refusal by the people of the town was due to stinginess, for which they were sinful.

﴿And they found in it a wall about to collapse﴾. That is, it nearly collapsed. This is a figurative expression, like one who is about to do something, as in the words of the poet:

"The spear wants the chest of Abu Bara'
and turns away from the blood of Banu 'Uqayl."

The meaning of yanqadd is that it falls quickly, and yunaqid means that it splits lengthwise.

Yahya ibn Ya'mur recited yuridu an yanqusa with the unpointed sad, from al-nuqsan (decrease, deterioration).

﴿So he set it up﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: he set up the wall with his hand, and it stood straight. The root of jadr is "to appear," and from it comes al-judari (smallpox), because of how it appears on the skin.

Musa, peace be upon him, was amazed, since they had asked the people of the town for food and they had refused to entertain them as guests, yet he set up the wall for them. So he said: ﴿If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it﴾. Qatadah said: the worst of towns is the one that does not host guests and does not respect the rights of the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿He said, "This is the parting between me and you"﴾. There are two interpretations of this. The first: this which you have said is "the parting between me and you." The second: this time is "the parting between me and you."

﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not hold patience﴾. This may have two meanings. The first: you could not be patient in witnessing it. The second: you could not be patient in refraining from asking about it.

Ibn 'Abbas narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "May Allah have mercy on Musa. Had he been patient, he would have acquired from him a thousand lessons."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verse 79:

(p-332) His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿As for the ship, it belonged to poor people﴾. In calling them "masakin" (poor), there are four aspects. The first: because of their poverty and need.

The second: because of the severe hardship they endured at sea, as one says of someone who has suffered hardship, "This miskin has met with great toil."

The third: because of the disability and ailments they had.

The fourth: because of the weakness of their resources and their inability to defend themselves, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A miskin is a man who has no wife" (miskin rajul la imra'a lahu). He called him miskin because of his weakness of resources and his inability to take care of himself, not because of his poverty and indigence.

Some of the leading reciters read "limasakkin" with a shadda on the sin (lamasakkin), and al-masakkun are "those who hold on" (al-mumsikun). Regarding the interpretation of this there are two views. The first: they were holding on to their ship in order to work on it themselves.

The second: those who hold on to their wealth out of miserliness, so they do not spend it.

﴿So I wished to damage it﴾, meaning, I wished to cause a defect in it.

﴿And behind them was a king﴾. Regarding His saying "behind them (wara'ahum) a king," there are two views. The first: that it means "in front of them" (khalfahum), and their return would be past him without their knowing about him. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: that it means "in front of them" (amamahum).

Ibn Abbas used to read: "wa kana amamahum malikun" (and in front of them was a king). The grammarians differed on the use of wara' in place of amam, in three sayings. The first: its use is permissible in every situation and every place, and it is one of the words with contrary meanings (min al-adad). God, exalted is He, said: ﴿From behind them (min wara'ihim) is Hell﴾, meaning, from in front of them and before them is Hell. The poet said:

Do the sons of Marwan hope for my hearing and obedience, while my people are Tamim and the wilderness is wara'iya (behind me)?

meaning amami (in front of me).

The second: that wara' may be used in place of amam with regard to times and periods, because a person may pass through them, so they become behind him; but it is not used for other things.

It is said that the name of the king was Hudad ibn Budad, and Muqatil said his name was Mindalah ibn Jalandi ibn Sa'd al-Azdi.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 80–81:

It was said that the boy was "sudasi" (about sixteen years old), and it was said that by "sudasi" he meant one who was sixteen years old. It was also said that rather he meant that his height was six spans. This was related by al-Kalbi. The boy was a highwayman who would cut off the road between the village of his father and the village of his mother, and the people of both villages would support him and protect him from [punishment].

Qatadah said: His parents rejoiced at him when he was born, and grieved over him when he was killed; had he lived, their ruin would have been in him.

It was said that the name of the boy was Jaysur.

Muqatil said: The name of his father was Kazir, and the name of his mother was Sahwa.

The second: its meaning is: "Your Lord feared that the boy would overwhelm his parents with rebellion and disbelief," so he expressed fear by the word "khashyah." Muqatil said: In the recitation of Ubayy it reads: "Your Lord feared." The fear here is a metaphor, being negated of Allah, exalted is He.

The third: Al-Khidr disliked that the boy would overwhelm his parents by his rebellion and disbelief, sin and wrongdoing. Thus, in "khashyah" here there are three interpretations: the first, that it means knowledge; the second, that it means fear; the third, that it means dislike.

In ﴿overwhelm them (yurhiqahuma)﴾ there are two interpretations: the first, that it means "to support/provide for them," related by Ibn Zayd; the second, that it means "to burden them," from "al-rahaq," which is hardship.

His mother was pregnant and then gave birth. Regarding what she bore there are two opinions: the first, she bore a righteous Muslim boy, related by Ibn Jurayj.

(p-335) The second, she bore a girl whom a prophet married, and she gave birth to a prophet through whose hands Allah guided a nation among the nations.

﴿And nearer in mercy (ruhman)﴾ Regarding this there are three interpretations: the first, meaning more dutiful to his parents than the one who was killed, related by Qatadah, who took "ruhm" to mean righteousness (al-birr). From this is the saying of the poet:

"A rejected one whom Yazid overtook with mercy, and he did not find, among his favours, anything unattainable."

"And how [could there be] wronging of a girl, and in her is gentleness and ruhm?"

"More tender and merciful than a mother towards her only child, and braver than a lion of thick mane that hunts."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verse 82:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿As for the wall, it belonged to two orphan boys in the city﴾. Muqatil claimed that the names of the two boys were Sirm and Sarim, the name of their father was Kashikh, and the name of their mother was Rihna, and that the city was a village called ʿIdashi.

The literal meaning of "wall" (jidar) is that which encloses a house so as to prevent entry and protect its structure; it is used figuratively for the walls of other things.

(p-336) ﴿Beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾. Regarding this treasure there are three opinions. The first: it was sheets of knowledge (suhuf ʿilm), said by Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and Mujahid.

The second: it was a tablet of gold on which wisdoms were inscribed. This was said by al-Hasan. Ibn al-Kalbi related from Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "﴿Beneath it was a treasure belonging to them﴾: the treasure was a tablet of gold on which was written: 'In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate. Wonder at the one who believes in death, how can he rejoice? Wonder at the one who is certain of destiny, how can he grieve? Wonder at the one who is certain of the passing of this world and its changing of its people, how can he feel at ease with it? There is no god but Allah; Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.'"

﴿Their father was righteous, so your Lord willed that they should reach their maturity and extract their treasure﴾. The scholars differed concerning the continued life of al-Khidr (ʿalayhi al-salam) until today. One group held that he remains alive, because he drank from the Spring of Life.

(p-337) Remaining.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 83–84:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They ask you about Dhu al-Qarnayn﴾. It is disputed whether he was a prophet (nabi). Some people held that he was a prophet sent (mab'uth), through whose hand God opened the earth. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "He was neither a prophet nor an angel, but he was a righteous servant (ʿabd salih) who loved God and whom God loved, and a sincere advisor to God, so God gave him sincere counsel. His people struck him on his one horn, and he remained for as long as God willed; then he called them to guidance, and they struck him on his other horn. He did not have two horns like the horns of a bull."

As for the reason he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn (the Two-Horned), there are four opinions:

The first: because he had two horns on the sides of his head, as ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, related.

The second: because he had two braids (dafira), and he was named after them. This was said by al-Hasan.

The third: because he reached the two extremities of the earth, east and west, and so he was named for his dominion over the "two horns of the earth" (qarnay al-ard). This was said by al-Zuhri.

The fourth: because he saw in his dream that he drew near the sun until he took hold of its two horns at its rising and its setting, so he related his vision to his people, and he was named Dhu al-Qarnayn. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

Ibn ʿAbbas related that Dhu al-Qarnayn was ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Dahhak ibn Maʿadd. Muhammad ibn Ishaq related that he was a man from the people of Egypt named Marzuban ibn Mardaba al-Yunani, son of Yunan ibn Yafith ibn Nuh.

Muʿadh ibn Jabal said: He was a Roman whose name was al-Iskandarus.

Ibn Hisham said: He is al-Iskandar, the one who built Alexandria.

(p-338) His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, We established him in the earth﴾ may bear two meanings: First: by his conquest of its dominion. Second: by his management of its affairs.

﴿And We gave him of every thing a way (sabab)﴾. In it there are two meanings: First: of every thing, knowledge through which he attained his aim, said by Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah. Second: what he used to obtain audience with kings, to kill enemies, and to conquer lands.

It may also bear a third meaning: We made for him in every land that he ruled authority (sultan) and awe (hayba).

The second: it means black clay, as said by Ka'b.

Thus a third view arises. It is not impossible that this describes the spring, that it be murky, black and hot. It has been transmitted on the authority of Tubba''s poetry, where he described Dhu al-Qarnayn in a way that agrees with this, saying:

Tha'th means silt.
Harmad means black.

﴿So shall we pay you a tribute on condition that you set up a barrier between us and them?﴾ Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited ﴿kharājan﴾, and the rest recited ﴿kharjan﴾. Regarding the difference between the two recitations there are three aspects. The first: al-kharāj is the produce (ghallah), and al-kharj is the wage (ujrah).

The second: al-kharāj is a noun for what comes out of the land, and al-kharj is what is taken from the necks (of people). This was said by Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala'.

The third: al-kharj is what is taken in one payment, and al-kharāj is fixed and taken every year. This was said by Tha'lab.

His statement, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿He said, "What my Lord has established me in is better"﴾, meaning it is better than the wage you offer me.

﴿So help me with strength﴾. Regarding this there are two aspects. The first: with implements (bi-ālah), said by al-Kalbi. The second: with men (bi-rijāl), said by Muqatil.

﴿I will set up a barrier (radman) between you and them﴾. Regarding this there are two aspects. The first: it is a strong partition. The second: it is a barrier made of layers piled upon one another, which is greater than a barrier (sadd).

﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾. Regarding this there are three sayings. The first: they are pieces of iron, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid.

The second: it is split iron (fil'q al-ḥadīd), said by Qatadah.

The third: it is gathered iron, and from this comes the word zabūr (scripture), because its letters are gathered in writing. Tubba' al-Yamani said:

I have endured so that they may know, and around them, blocks of iron, evening and day.

﴿Until, when he made level between the two cliffs﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak said: the two ṣadafān are two mountains. 'Amr ibn Shas said:

Both cliffs, its light penetrates them, blazing like a lamp in darkness.

Regarding them there are two aspects. The first: each of them faces its companion, derived from ṣudfah (meeting face to face) in encounter. This was said by al-Azhari.

The second, said by Ibn 'Isa: they are two mountains, each separated from the other, as if it had turned away from it.

Then there are two aspects. The first: al-ṣadafān is a name for the peaks of the two mountains. The second: it is a name for what lies between the two mountains.

The meaning of His statement ﴿made level between the two cliffs﴾ is that, with what he placed between them, he covered their peaks and leveled them.

﴿He said, "Blow"﴾, that is, into the fire of the iron.

﴿Until, when he made it fire﴾, meaning molten like fire in heat and flame.

﴿He said, "Bring me, I will pour over it molten copper"﴾. Regarding ﴿qiṭr﴾ there are four aspects. The first: qiṭr is copper (nuḥās), said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah, and al-Dahhak.

The second: it is lead, related by Ibn al-Anbari.

The third: it is melted brass (ṣufr), said by Muqatil. From this is the verse of al-Huṭay'ah:

And he put into cauldrons of iron pots of brass, not of earthenware.

The fourth: it is melted iron, said by Abu 'Ubaydah, who recited:

A sword like the color of salt, its iron has become hot from the melted iron that is pierced.

Its stones were iron, and its mortar was copper.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 97–99:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So they were not able to scale it﴾, meaning they could not rise above it.

﴿Nor could they make a breach in it﴾, meaning from its base. This is the view of Qatadah. It was also said that the barrier lies beyond the Sea of Rum, between two mountains there, whose far ends are bordered by the Encompassing Ocean.

It was also said: the height of the barrier is two hundred cubits, its width about fifty cubits, and it is made of iron, almost solid.

It has been narrated that a man said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "I have seen the barrier." He said: "Describe it." He said: "It is like striped cloth (burd muhabbar), its paths are black and its paths are red." He said: "You have seen it."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He said: "This is a mercy from my Lord"﴾ may bear two meanings. The first: that his work is a mercy from Allah, the Exalted, to His servants. The second: that his power to accomplish it is a mercy from Allah, the Exalted, to him.

(p-345) ﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level (dakka'); and the promise of my Lord is always true﴾. Ibn Mas'ud said: this will happen after 'Isa, peace be upon him, kills the Dajjal, in a marfu' hadith.

It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: "They will toil at their digging during the day, until when evening comes and they almost see the rays of the sun, they say: 'We will return tomorrow and dig its remainder.' Then they return the next day and it has become as it was, until when the command of Allah comes they say: 'Tomorrow, if Allah wills, we will breach its remainder.' They return to it and breach it by the permission of Allah, and they come out from it upon the people from their fortresses. Then they shoot arrows into the sky, and the arrows return to them stained like blood. They say: 'We have prevailed over the people of the earth and overcome the people of the sky.' Then Allah, the Exalted, sends upon them what destroys them."

﴿So when the promise of my Lord comes﴾: concerning this there are two views. The first: the Day of Resurrection; this was said by Ibn Bahr. The second: it is the appointed term at which they will come out.

﴿He will make it level (dakka')﴾, meaning the barrier. Concerning dakka' there are three meanings. The first: ground (ardan), said by Qutrub. The second: pieces (qit'an), said by al-Kalbi. The third: demolition until it is leveled into the ground and becomes even with it, said by al-Akhfash. From this is the saying of al-Aghlab:

Is there none but a departing one who leveled a cave so that it collapsed?

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We will leave some of them that day surging over one another﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions. The first: they are the people whom Dhu al-Qarnayn mentioned, on the day the barrier is opened, surging over one another. (p-346) The second: the disbelievers on the Day of Resurrection, surging over one another. The third: they are humans and jinn at the opening of the barrier.

Concerning the word there are two meanings. The first: some of them mix with others. The second: some of them push others away, derived from the surging of the sea.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verses 100–102:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Those whose eyes were in a covering from My remembrance﴾ admits of two meanings. One of them: misguidance is like a covering over their eyes, preventing them from recalling the retribution.

The second: they were heedless of taking lesson from His power, which necessitates remembering Him.

﴿And they were not able to hear⁠ ⁠—﴾ regarding this there are two meanings. One of them: the intended meaning of "hearing" here is intellect, and its sense is "they did not understand."

The second: it is to be taken literally, as hearing with the ears.

Regarding this (the phrase "they were not able") there are two meanings. One of them: they were not able to do it out of burden (istithqal, finding it heavy).

The second: out of abhorrence (maqt).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as a welcome (nuzul)﴾. Regarding this there are two interpretations. One of them: the nuzul is food, so Hell was made a meal for them. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: that it is a dwelling-place (manzil). This was said by al-Zajjaj.(p-347)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 18, verse 103–106:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Say: Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in respect of deeds?﴾ There are five opinions concerning them. The first: they are the priests (qissisun) and the monks (ruhban). This was said by ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.

The second: they are the People of the Book, the Jews and the Christians. This was said by Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas.

The third: they are the people of Harura' (Harurites) from among the Kharijites (Khawarij, a early sectarian group). This is related from ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him.

The fourth: they are the people of desires (ahl al-ahwa', those who follow innovated and deviant inclinations).

The fifth: they are those who perform good deeds and then lay claim to them with reproach (yamunnu).

And it is possible that there is a sixth: they are the hypocrites who oppose in their beliefs what they show in their deeds.

And it is possible that there is a seventh: they are those who seek the worldly life and abandon the Hereafter.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We shall not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Concerning this there are four aspects. The first: because of their humiliation before Allah, the Exalted, due to their sins that they committed, they become despised, having no weight.

The second: because of their lightness through ignorance and their folly through foolishness, they become like those who have no weight.

The third: that sins take away their weight, until they do not weigh anything of their lightness.

It is narrated from Kaʿb that he said: A man will be brought on the Day of Resurrection and weighed against a grain, and he will not weigh it; he will be weighed against the wing of a mosquito, and he will not weigh it. Then he recited: ﴿So We shall not assign them any weight on the Day of Resurrection﴾.

The fourth: that their good deeds are nullified by disbelief, so their evil deeds remain. Thus the weighing will be against them, not in their favour.

The Word of the Exalted, the Majestic: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds, for them are the Gardens of Paradise (al-Firdaws) as a welcoming provision﴾. Regarding ﴿al-Firdaws﴾ there are five opinions. The first: al-Firdaws is the middle of Paradise and its most excellent place. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: it is the highest part of Paradise and the finest of it. Damrah narrated it as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet ﷺ).

The third: it is the garden in Roman (Greek) language. This was said by Mujahid.

The fourth: it is the garden that gathers the beauties of every garden. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The fifth: it is the garden in which there are grapevines. This was said by Ka'b.

The wording of the term has been disputed, with four opinions. The first: it is Arabic, and the Arabs mentioned it in their poetry. This was said by Tha'lab.

The second: it is Roman (Greek). This was said by Mujahid.

The third: it is Nabataean, *firdasan*. This was said by al-Suddi.

The fourth: it is Syriac. This was said by Abu Salih.

(p-349) The Word of the Exalted, the Majestic: ﴿Abiding therein forever; they will not desire any removal from it﴾. That is, *mutahawwilan* (a place of transfer). In it there are three aspects. The first: *badalan* (a substitute, an exchange). This was said by al-Dahhak.

The second: *tahwilan* (a change). This was said by Muqatil.

The third: *hilah* (a means or stratagem), meaning they will not seek to devise another dwelling other than it. The word here is *hiwalan* (حِوَلا), which the commentators explain according to the above senses.

It is also said that the first of them to enter (Paradise) will say: "Allah only admitted me first among them because there is no one more excellent than me." And the last of them to enter will say: "Allah only delayed me because there is no one to whom Allah has given the like of what He has given me."

It is also said that the first of them to enter (Paradise) will say: "Allah only admitted me first among them because there is no one more excellent than me." And the last of them to enter will say: "Allah only delayed me because there is no one to whom Allah has given the like of what He has given me."

The Exalted's saying: ﴿Say: Even if the sea were ink for the words of my Lord﴾. On this there are three opinions.

The first: it is a promise of reward for the one who obeys Him, and a threat of punishment for the one who disobeys Him. Ibn Bahr said this, and similar to it is ﴿the sea would be exhausted before the words of my Lord are exhausted﴾.

The second: it is the knowledge of the Qur'an. Mujahid said this.

The third: this was said by God, Exalted is He, to show how far His creatures are from being able to count His acts and His known things, even though they are established and counted with Him.

The Exalted said: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds﴾. On this there are three interpretations:

First: it means, "whoever fears the meeting with his Lord." This is the view of Muqatil and Qutrub.

Second: whoever hopes (*yaʼmul*) for the meeting with his Lord.

Third: whoever believes in (*yuṣaddiq bi*) the meeting with his Lord. This is the view of al-Kalbi.

(p-350) Regarding "the meeting with his Lord," there are two interpretations. The first is that its meaning is the meeting with his Lord's reward. This is the view of Saʻid ibn Jubayr.

The second: whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, affirming that he will be resurrected to Him and will stand before Him.

﴿Let him do righteous deeds﴾. On this there are three interpretations. The first is that it means deeds sincere, free from *riyaʼ* (showing off to people). This is the view of Dhu al-Nun al-Misri.

The second: that he meets God with it without being ashamed before Him. This is the view of Yahya ibn Muʻadh.

The third: that he avoids sins and performs acts of obedience.

﴿And let him not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾. On this there are two interpretations. The first is that *shirk* (association of partners with God) in His worship is disbelief (*kufr*), and its meaning is that no one else is worshipped alongside Him. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second is that it is *riyaʼ*, and its meaning is: he does not show off his deed to anyone. This is the view of Saʻid ibn Jubayr and Mujahid.

It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The thing I fear most for my community is *shirk* and hidden desire." It was said: "Will your community associate partners with God after you?" He said: "No, but indeed they will not worship sun, moon, stone, or idol; rather they will show off with their deeds." It was said: "O Messenger of God, is that *shirk*?" He said: "Yes." It was said: "And what is the hidden desire?" He said: "One of them rises in the morning fasting, then a worldly desire presents itself to him, so he breaks his fast for it and abandons his fast."

Al-Kalbi and Muqatil relate that this verse was revealed concerning Jundub ibn Zuhayr al-ʻAmiri, who came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said to him: "Indeed we perform a deed seeking the face of God, but then it is praised because of it, and that pleases us. And indeed I pray a prayer and lengthen it, hoping that it will be praised because of it." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Indeed God, the Exalted, says: I am the best partner. Whoever associates with Me in a deed he performs for Me, any of My creation, I abandon him and that partner." And this verse was revealed concerning him: ﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord, let him do righteous deeds, and let him not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) recited it to him.

It was also said that it is the last verse revealed of the Qur'an.
